objectives.title: Propositional logic, predicates and quantifiers
objectives.description: Express claims with connectives and quantifiers while preserving domain and scope.

objectives.title: Sets, relations and functions

lessons.title: Say exactly what you mean: logic and quantifiers
lessons.body: Start with ordinary claims about a small group. The meaning changes when we switch from 'every' to 'at least one'. Learn to preserve the domain and the order of quantifiers before using symbols.
lessons.historical_context: Euclid's definitions and propositions show why mathematical arguments depend on precise statements. Modern predicate logic makes quantifier scope explicit.

stages.prompt: Imagine a group containing two people: one owns a bicycle and one does not. Decide whether 'everyone owns a bicycle' and 'someone owns a bicycle' are true.
Compare 'every student solved a problem' with 'there is a problem every student solved'. Do these say the same thing? Explain the difference.
Draw a small domain of objects and mark which satisfy a predicate. Show how 'all' and 'some' select different patterns.
Rewrite a claim using 'for every' or 'there exists'. State the domain and the property being tested.
Represent 'every x in D has property P' and 'some x in D has property P' using quantifier notation. Then negate each statement.

exercise.objective: Translate quantified statements and preserve their logical scope.
exercise.prompt: Let D = {1,2,3,4} and P(x) mean 'x is even'. State whether (1) every x in D satisfies P, (2) some x in D satisfies P, and (3) no x in D satisfies P. Write each claim symbolically and negate the second claim correctly.
hints: List the elements of D and evaluate P for each one.
'Every' fails if even one counterexample exists; 'some' succeeds if at least one witness exists.
To negate 'there exists x such that P(x)', write 'for every x, not P(x)'.

rubric.description: Correctly distinguishes universal and existential claims.
Gives correct truth values and a valid witness or counterexample.
Negates the existential statement with the correct quantifier and predicate.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Write and negate a statement about every node in a network having at least one neighbor. State what an isolated node would show.

lessons.title: Sets, relations and functions
lessons.body: Use collections of objects to distinguish membership, subset, relation and function. A function is a special relation: each input in its declared domain has exactly one output in its codomain.
lessons.historical_context: Set language became a shared foundation for modern mathematics. The lesson focuses on the practical distinction between a general relation and a single-valued mapping.

stages.prompt: Make two groups of cards: students and books. Draw arrows from each student to the books they borrowed.
Can one student point to two books? Can one student point to no book? What changes if the arrows represent a function assigning each student exactly one locker?
Draw a mapping diagram with a domain on the left and codomain on the right. Compare a many-to-one function with a relation that gives one input two outputs.
Define domain, codomain, image, relation and function in your own words. Give one example that is a relation but not a function.
Represent a function f from A to B and state the condition that each element of A has exactly one image in B.

exercise.objective: Classify relations and explain when a relation is a function.
exercise.prompt: Let A = {a,b,c} and B = {1,2,3}. Consider R = {(a,1),(b,2),(c,2)} and S = {(a,1),(a,2),(b,3)}. Decide whether each is a function from A to B. Explain using the domain rule, then give one relation that is not a function because an input has no output.
hints: Check every element of A, not only the elements that appear in the ordered pairs.
A function cannot assign two different outputs to the same input.
A relation can be incomplete or multi-valued; those are not functions from the full declared domain.

rubric.description: States the one-output rule for every domain element.
Correctly classifies R and S from their ordered pairs.
Constructs a valid non-function example and explains why it fails.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Model a program that maps each user ID to a single account record. Give an example of data that violates the function contract.

lessons.title: Graphs, paths and trees
lessons.body: A graph models relationships. Vertices represent objects and edges represent connections. Paths describe movement through the graph; cycles return to a previously visited vertex. A tree is a connected graph with no cycles.
lessons.historical_context: Graph theory grew from concrete route and network problems, including Euler's work on the bridges of Königsberg. The lesson turns a map into a precise combinatorial object.

stages.prompt: Draw four places as dots and connect pairs that have a direct road. Do not worry about distances yet.
Find a route from one place to another. Does any route revisit a place? Can you find a closed route that returns to its start?
Label vertices and edges. Draw one path, one cycle, and a connected graph with no cycle.
Explain the difference between a path, a cycle, a connected graph and a tree. State whether every tree is connected.
Represent the graph as a vertex set V and edge set E. Write an adjacency list for your example.
Implement a small graph traversal or manually trace breadth-first search from a chosen start vertex. Record the visited order.

exercise.objective: Represent a network as a graph and reason about paths, cycles and trees.
exercise.prompt: Use V = {A,B,C,D} and E = {{A,B},{B,C},{C,D}}. Write an adjacency list, give a path from A to D, and explain why this graph is a tree. Then add edge {A,D} and identify the cycle created.
hints: An undirected edge appears in both endpoint adjacency lists.
The original graph is connected and has no closed path with distinct intermediate vertices.
The added edge connects the two ends of the existing path and closes a cycle.

rubric.description: Builds the correct adjacency list and path.
Explains connectedness and absence of cycles in the original graph.
Identifies the cycle after adding the new edge.
Explains how the model could represent a real network.

exercise.transfer_prompt: Model a dependency network between software modules. Explain what a cycle would mean and why it may block a valid build order.

rubric.description: Distinguishes quantifiers and scope.
Correctly reasons with witnesses and counterexamples.
Negates a quantified statement correctly.
Explains relation and function conditions.
Classifies mappings from ordered pairs.
Applies the function contract to a new example.
Represents a graph with vertices, edges and adjacency lists.
Reasons about paths and cycles.
Justifies tree properties.
Maps the graph idea to a dependency network.
